inline.s: Question: How does one awaken to this and then guard it?
Answer: It is what the Xiu Xin Jue (Treatise on the Contemplation of Mind)
says in its later passage:
“Therefore, after awakening one must always
keep watch
, for when deluded thoughts suddenly arise, one does not follow them at all. Reduce and reduce again, until reaching non-doing
(at this stage of non-doing, even without watching, thoughts arise and are not followed)
, and only then is it ultimate. This is what the world’s good teachers mean by
‘after awakening, tending the ox’
The Biyan Lu (Blue Cliff Record) records:
Mazu was walking with his disciple Baizhang when they saw a wild duck fly past. The patriarch said: “What is that?” Baizhang said: “A wild duck.” The patriarch said: “Where has it gone
(testing whether Baizhang dwells in form and gives rise to mind)
? Baizhang said: “It has flown away.” Thereupon the patriarch twisted Baizhang’s nose, and Baizhang cried out in pain. The patriarch said:
When did it ever fly away!
At these words Baizhang had an awakening
(xǐng: Baizhang awakened at his master’s words)

Baizhang’s first reply, “a wild duck,” was like a mirror reflecting an object—that was correct. But his second reply, “it has flown away,” was to dwell in form and give rise to mind, to chase things as conditions shift, and not to guard the original mind (losing right mindfulness). That is why Mazu twisted his nose: to make him turn back and guard the original mind. In the midst of the pain Baizhang heard his master say, “When did it ever fly away?” (The wild duck is an illusion—how could there be coming or going?) He was suddenly awakened:
“Thus should one give rise to the pure mind.”
(Mazu twisted Baizhang’s nose precisely to make him
never forget to guard the original mind
, and not chase things as conditions shift.)

[Baizhang: Dazhi Chanshi Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou during the Tang dynasty, a dharma heir of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi. The Master was the first to establish the rules and forms of the Chan gate, the so-called “Baizhang Monastic Rules.”] [When did it ever fly away: to gather characteristics back into the nature and empty them all.]
[Gathering characteristics back into the nature: to dissolve the myriad phenomena into the true reality of all dharmas, seeing only the unborn within apparent arising and ceasing. (For details see
“The True Reality of All Dharmas”
for the full discussion.)
All that has characteristics is false and deceptive.”

If one does not detach from characteristics, it is hard to awaken to the Way. Hence Mazu used the thunderbolt method of lightning that leaves no time to cover the ears, striking at Baizhang’s unawakened mind. The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra says:
“The Dharma of ‘if one loses the original mind, one should at once repent’—this is coolness and clarity.”
From this we may glimpse the conduct of a strict master and a worthy disciple, and feel intimately the truth that “plum blossom fragrance comes from the bitter cold.”
The Wudeng Huiyuan (Compendium of Five Lamps) says:
“The Master
(Baizhang)

was attending Mazu on a walk when they saw a flock of wild ducks fly past. The patriarch said: ‘What is that?’ The Master said: ‘A wild duck.’ The patriarch said: ‘Where has it gone?’ The Master said: ‘It has flown away.’ The patriarch then twisted the Master’s nose, and he cried out in pain. The patriarch said: ‘And you still say it has flown away!’ At these words the Master had an awakening. He returned to the attendants’ quarters and wept bitterly. A fellow monk asked: ‘Are you thinking of your parents
(in ancient usage the same as ‘ye,’ the questioning particle)

?’ The Master said: ‘No.’ ‘Has someone scolded you?’ The Master said: ‘No.’ ‘Why then are you crying?’ The Master said: ‘My nose was twisted by the Master and still aches unbearably.’ The fellow monk said: ‘What cause is it that does not accord?’ The Master said: ‘Go ask the Master.’ The fellow monk asked the Master: ‘What cause does the attendant Hai have that does not accord, that he weeps in the quarters? I beg the Master to tell me
(myself)
.’ The Master said: ‘
He
(he)
understands
(has grasped it)

Go and ask him yourself.’ The fellow monk returned to the quarters and said: ‘The Master says you understand, and told me to ask you myself.’ The Master then burst out laughing. The fellow monk said: ‘A moment ago you were crying—why now do you laugh?’ The Master said: ‘A moment ago I cried; now I laugh.’ The fellow monk was bewildered. The next day Mazu ascended the hall. The assembly had just gathered when the Master came forward and rolled up the mat
(rolled up the bowing mat)

. The patriarch then descended from the seat, and the Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters. The patriarch said: ‘I said not a word just now—why did you roll up the mat?’ The Master said: ‘Yesterday the Master twisted my nose and it hurt.’ The patriarch said: ‘Where were you keeping your attention yesterday?’ The Master said: ‘Today my nose does not hurt again.’ The patriarch said: ‘
You deeply understand yesterday’s matter.
’ The Master bowed and withdrew.”

[“And you still say it has flown away”: here Mazu is instructing Baizhang that one should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects! Baizhang’s first reply, “a wild duck,” was like a mirror reflecting an object—that was correct. But his second reply, “it has flown away,” was to dwell in form and give rise to mind, to chase things as conditions shift, and not to guard the original mind (losing right mindfulness). That is why Mazu twisted his nose: to make him turn back and guard the original mind. In the midst of the pain Baizhang heard Mazu rebuke him: “And you still say it has flown away!” (The wild duck is an illusion—how could there be coming or going?) He was suddenly awakened: “Thus should one give rise to the pure mind.” (Mazu twisted Baizhang’s nose precisely to make him never forget to guard the original mind. One must not chase things as conditions shift; rather, one must gather characteristics back into the nature and empty them all.)]
The Diamond Sutra says:

“All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to the pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor should they give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; they should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all.”
Question: Why did Baizhang weep bitterly, and why did he laugh heartily?

Answer: What he wept over so bitterly was this: since beginningless kalpas, simply for not knowing “to gather characteristics back into the nature and guard the original mind,” he had suffered every torment to no purpose and been sunk in saṃsāra until now. What he laughed over so heartily was this: now that he had received this wondrous Dharma, he need only apply himself earnestly, and in this very life he would surely attain the fruit. This is truly the greatest of joyful events—at last he can return to the source of all that is! It is exactly as it is said: No other practice does practice require / but knowing where the road’s head lies; / once the road’s head is truly known, / both birth and death at once are gone.

Our goal is to break through the final pass and cut off afflictions (greed, anger, and delusion); the Confucian goal is to perfect benevolence, and its method of cultivation is very much worth learning from. The Analects,
Yan Yuan chapter, records:

“Yan Yuan asked about benevolence. The Master said: ‘To subdue oneself and return to propriety is benevolence. If for a single day one subdues oneself and returns to propriety, the whole world will return to benevolence. Benevolence proceeds from oneself—how could it proceed from others?’ Yan Yuan said: ‘May I ask its particulars?’ The Master said: ‘Do not look at what is contrary to propriety; do not listen to what is contrary to propriety; do not speak what is contrary to propriety; do not move in ways contrary to propriety.’ Yan Yuan said: ‘Though I am not quick-witted, I beg to put these words into practice.’”
(Translation: Once Yan Hui, a disciple of Confucius, asked how the state of benevolence could be attained. Confucius replied: To restrain oneself so that one’s conduct accords with propriety (
norms of conduct

) is benevolence. If one day you truly accomplish this—following the desires of your heart without overstepping the mark—then all under heaven will acknowledge that you have attained benevolence. Attaining benevolence rests wholly with yourself, not with others. Yan Hui then asked: So how should one do it concretely? Confucius answered: What is contrary to propriety, do not look at, do not listen to, do not speak of, do not do. Hearing this, Yan Hui said to his teacher: Though I am not clever enough, I am resolved to act according to the Master’s words.)
[Subduing oneself and returning to propriety: to restrain oneself and conform to the norms of conduct (to return to propriety). “Propriety” means the norms of conduct.]
Following this model, we have the following questions and answers:
Question: How is one to cut off afflictions?

Answer: Subdue oneself and return to principle. Restrain yourself and conform to principle. The “principle” here is the standard for body, speech, and mind: no greed, no anger, no delusion. If one day you truly accomplish being free and at ease while free of greed, anger, and delusion, then all under heaven will acknowledge that you have cut off afflictions. Cutting off afflictions rests wholly with yourself, not with others.
[Subduing oneself and returning to principle: to restrain oneself and conform to principle. The “principle” here is the standard for body, speech, and mind: no greed, no anger, no delusion.]
Question: So how should one do it concretely?

Answer: Do not look at what is contrary to principle; do not listen to what is contrary to principle; do not speak what is contrary to principle; do not act contrary to principle; do not think what is contrary to principle. The “principle” here is the standard for body, speech, and mind: no greed, no anger, no delusion. “Contrary to principle” means greed, anger, and delusion. These “five do-nots” mean: whatever would stir greed, anger, and delusion in you—do not look at it, do not listen to it, do not speak of it, do not do it, do not think of it.

Therefore, in breaking through the heavy pass, one must subdue oneself and return to principle: do not look at what is contrary to principle, do not listen to it, do not speak of it, do not act on it, do not think of it, and do not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects. Thus one subdues afflictions and prevents them from arising. When the six faculties meet the six objects, one needs the power of concentration (which is cultivated and trained) to hold oneself steady (this too is trained—hence the need for practice), to do what people find hard to do, to endure what people find hard to endure. Practice is the practice of endurance. As it is said, “Forbearance is a priceless treasure”; only one who can endure can attain true happiness. When circumstances arise, endure them; accept hardship; however unbearable, grit your teeth and hold firm. Once the hard pass is crossed, you gain freedom.
To end birth and death, one must know the root of birth and death and how to uproot it. The patriarch taught:
The root of birth and death is the three poisons—greed, anger, and delusion; and to uproot it is to spare no effort in the single instant when this mind turns!

In the everyday circumstances before you—when wife and children gather, when relatives and friends come and go, where righteousness and profit, adversity and favor contend, before joy, anger, greed, and delusion have arisen—fix your gaze beforehand, truly and clearly, see what the root of birth and death is, and at once uproot it with all your strength.
All suffering arises from craving; therefore the way to end suffering is this: wherever craving arises, there uproot it and extinguish it.

[All suffering arises from craving: craving collects suffering (craving produces suffering); it is the root of suffering. Because of craving there is grasping, then karma-making, then the suffering of retribution, then saṃsāra. Craving arises where the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) meet the six objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, mental objects). Therefore the key is to guard the gates of the six faculties tightly: when contact with objects occurs, raise clear awareness and cut off the root of delusion.]
For this, one must do the work of “not letting a single thought slip past, penetrating every thought.”

Not letting a single thought slip past is true practice; penetrating every thought is true awakening. Chan inquiry is only about finding an ultimate way out at the critical juncture of birth and death—not about seeking, apart from this, some extraordinary thing among ink, paper, words, and the teachings of the three vehicles and twelve divisions.
[Not letting it slip past: not being deceived by it.] [Penetrating it: not being shrouded by it, not being toyed with by it, not taking it as something real.]
In the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, the Buddha says:

“Monks, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is craving, which brings renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Monks, and where does this craving arise and become established? In the world, wherever there is the attractive and the pleasing, there craving arises and becomes established. And in the world, what is the attractive and the pleasing? In the world, the eye is attractive and pleasing; there craving arises and becomes established. In the world, the ear is attractive and pleasing; there craving arises and becomes established. … Monks, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its abandonment, relinquishment, liberation, and non-attachment. But monks, where is craving to be uprooted, where is it to be extinguished? In the world, wherever there is the attractive and the pleasing—there craving is to be uprooted and extinguished. And in the world, what is the attractive and the pleasing? In the world, the eye is attractive and pleasing; there craving is to be uprooted and extinguished. In the world, the ear is attractive and pleasing; there craving is to be uprooted and extinguished. …”
(For details see
“The Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness” and its commentary

[Truth: a principle that is real and without error.] [The Four Noble Truths: the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. 1. The truth of suffering sets forth the truth that life is full of suffering. Suffering has the characteristic of oppression; suffering is the reality of actual life. 2. The “collection” in the truth of the origin of suffering means that which brings about and produces; it sets forth the truth of how the suffering of life comes to be. Life’s suffering comes from craving—hence grasping, hence karma-making, hence the suffering of retribution, hence saṃsāra. 3. The truth of cessation sets forth the truth of stilling all suffering. When all the collection of suffering (craving) is forever ended without remainder, with no grasping and no attachment, then there is no more karma-making, no more suffering, no more saṃsāra—this is the truth of cessation. 4. The truth of the path sets forth how to end forever the collection of suffering (craving), that is, the way to end suffering. Of the Four Noble Truths, origin is the cause and suffering the effect; the path is the cause and cessation the effect.] [Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence: craving in the realm of desire, craving in the realm of form, craving in the formless realm.] [Craving in the formless realm: in the formless realm there is no matter (no material dharmas), and therefore no body, palaces, or implements; only the knowing mind remains, dwelling in profound and subtle meditative absorption. The craving there is attachment to that profound absorption—delighting in it as pleasant and thus giving rise to clinging.]
Master Yinguang, in his Preface to Liaofan’s Four Lessons, gives a most penetrating teaching on subduing afflictions and even on cutting them off. It is excerpted and annotated below:

[Yet to become a sage is not difficult; it lies in making one’s bright virtue shine of itself. To make one’s bright virtue shine, one must begin with investigating things and extending knowledge. If the things of human desire cannot be thoroughly removed, then the true knowledge originally possessed can by no means be brought to full manifestation.]

Yet becoming a sage is not difficult either; it lies only in making manifest the bright and upright virtue of one’s own nature. To make manifest the bright and upright virtue of one’s own nature, one must begin with “removing the things of human desire and revealing the true knowledge originally possessed by the mind.” If the things of human desire cannot be thoroughly removed, then the true knowledge originally possessed can by no means be brought to full manifestation.

[Bright virtue: the bright and upright virtue of one’s own nature. It is inherent in everyone, but is sealed off and hidden by all kinds of unreasonable feelings and thoughts.] [Investigating things and extending knowledge: removing the things of human desire and revealing the true knowledge originally possessed by the mind. The Book of Rites,
Great Learning says: “Extending knowledge lies in investigating things; when things are investigated, knowledge is complete.”]

[If one wishes to bring true knowledge to manifestation, one should, in daily activity and speech, constantly raise clear awareness. Do not let any unreasonable feeling or thought briefly sprout in the mind. Constantly keep the mind empty, bright, and thoroughly clear—like a mirror on its stand, reflecting whatever comes before it. It only reflects the object before it and does not turn with it. Beauty or ugliness belongs to the other; what has it to do with me? Coming, it does not anticipate; going, it does not linger.]

If one wishes to bring true knowledge to manifestation, then in daily life—when thoughts stir and words and actions are made—one should constantly raise clear awareness. Do not let any emotion or thought that goes against principle sprout in the mind even briefly. One should constantly keep the mind empty, bright, and thoroughly clear, like a bright mirror on its stand: whatever appears before it is merely reflected, and one is not dragged around by it. Whether beautiful or ugly is their own affair—what has it to do with me? When they come, there is no expectation or waiting; when they go, there is no affliction or lingering.
These few sentences are the key to cultivating the mind: let the true mind be master.

[Speech and action: words and conduct.] [Clear awareness: clearly knowing what one’s present thought and emotion are. This is the basic skill for turning evil into good, turning delusion into awakening, and turning the ordinary person into a sage. Hence the patriarchs and great masters often said: at all times and in all places, whatever karma one creates with body, speech, and mind, one should look back and know that it is mind.] [Yan: beautiful.] [Chi
chī
: ugly.] [Yuji: that is, “to anticipate.”]

[If unreasonable feelings and thoughts begin to stir even slightly, one should sternly attack and wipe them out completely. It is like facing an enemy army: not only must one not let them invade one’s territory, one must also behead their generals, seize their banners, and annihilate the remaining band.]

If unreasonable feelings and thoughts have just begun to appear, one should at once sternly attack and wipe them out completely. It is like facing an enemy army: not only must one not let them invade one’s territory, one must also behead their generals, seize their banners, annihilate the remaining band, and pull them out by the roots.
[Beginning to stir: just beginning to appear.] [Fengjiang: a region entrusted to an official with full authority to administer it.] [Qian
qiān
: to seize.]
[The method of commanding the army must be strict self-governance: be neither indolent nor careless. Subdue the self and return to propriety; uphold reverence and preserve sincerity.]

The method of commanding the army must be strict self-governance. One must be neither indolent nor negligent, and must restrain one’s seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting so that they accord with the requirements of “propriety,” with reverence and sincerity.

[Wu: do not.] [Subduing the self and returning to propriety: the Confucian method of self-cultivation—restraining one’s seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting so that they accord with the requirements of “propriety.”] [Upholding reverence and preserving sincerity: outwardly reverent, inwardly sincere.]
[The weapons to be used must be Yanzi’s four do-nots, Zengzi’s three daily reflections, and Qu Boyu’s diminishing of faults and knowing of wrongs.]
The weapons to be used must be Yanzi’s four do-nots, Zengzi’s three daily reflections, and Qu Boyu’s diminishing of faults and knowing of wrongs.

[Weapons: arms.] [Yanzi’s four do-nots: Yanzi is Yan Hui, a disciple of Confucius. He excelled in the work of subduing the self, strictly observing: do not look at what is contrary to propriety, do not listen to what is contrary to propriety, do not speak what is contrary to propriety, do not move in ways contrary to propriety.] [Zengzi’s three reflections: Zengzi is Zeng Shen, a disciple of Confucius. He excelled in the work of self-examination, saying, “I examine myself three times a day”: whether in counseling others I have been unfaithful; whether in dealings with friends I have been insincere; whether I have practiced what I was taught—these three he closely examined in body and mind. [Qu
qú

Boyu: a minister of the state of Wei in the Spring and Autumn period, who daily examined himself, checked himself, and corrected his faults—day after day, year after year, never a day without finding that he still had faults, never a day without bitterly repenting and correcting them.] [Few faults: to diminish one’s own faults.] [Knowing wrongs: to know one’s own faults.]

[Add to this trembling caution, as if standing on the brink of a deep abyss, as if treading on thin ice, and face them so. Then the army’s might will spread far, and the band of thieves will be chilled with fear. Dreading the extreme punishment of extermination, they will hope to receive the great grace of pacification. From then on they will surrender one after another and submit to the highest transformation, wholly reforming their former minds and cultivating virtue thereafter.]

Add to this trembling caution—as if standing on the brink of a deep abyss, as if treading on thin ice—and face the enemy army (unreasonable feelings and thoughts) with the utmost caution and solemn order. Then the army’s might will spread far, and the band of thieves will be chilled with fear. Dreading the calamity of extermination, they will hope for the great grace of pardon and pacification. Thereupon they will surrender one after another, submit, turn their minds around, wash their hearts and renew their faces, and begin life anew.
[Zhan zhan jing jing: describes a manner of careful caution.] [
Band of thieves: here “band of thieves” refers to unreasonable feelings and thoughts.] [Li (lí): to suffer.] [Yuxiu jue de: to restore one’s virtue. “Yu
yù”
, a classical particle; “Jue
jué”
, meaning “his,” “its.”]

[The general does not go beyond the door, and the soldiers’ blades are not bloodied. All foes become newborn babes, and even the rebellious all become good citizens. Those above lead and those below follow; the whole land is clear and peaceful. Without moving shield or spear, one brings about great peace while sitting still.]

Thereupon the general does not go beyond the camp gate, the soldiers do not bleed in battle, and all foes and rebels become good and honest common people. The band of thieves, high and low, follow one another’s example and all turn from evil to right. The whole world is clear and tranquil; without fighting a battle, all under heaven is at great peace.
[Newborn babe: a newly born infant, usually used to liken one who is pure and good.] [Shuai tu: meaning “within the four seas.” “Shuai” is pronounced shuài and means “all,” “entirely.”]

This passage says that the key to attacking and governing unreasonable feelings and thoughts is: stand in strict formation and wait; the moment they begin to stir (this is the best moment to destroy the enemy), strike head-on at once and root them out. People create evil through the actions of body, speech, and mind, and body and speech are rooted in mind. Therefore clear awareness that cuts off evil is like felling a poisonous tree—cut straight through its root.

Because at this stage one is still dwelling in the present and observing the mind, deluded thoughts are few, and even when they arise one can notice them in time. Each thought that arises must be closely examined: is it greed, anger, or delusion? Why did it arise? Dig out each root one by one and root it out.
When one’s skill in protection has deepened, one must constantly observe and illumine throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, striving to accomplish:
Within, not turning with thoughts; without, not pulled by circumstances; not grasping at characteristics, and unmoved in suchness.
In doing this work, generally speaking, there are two paths:
1. As soon as a thought arises, be aware; once aware, it is gone. Master Guifeng says in the Preface to the Collected Writings on the Source of Chan:

“Awakening to the emptiness of all characteristics, the mind is naturally without thought. As soon as a thought arises, be aware; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.”

2. Because where there is awareness there are no deluded thoughts, one asks only whether awareness is continuous, not whether deluded thoughts arise. When there is movement, be aware of the movement; when there is no movement, anchor the mind on the dharma-realm.
If the mind scatters, immediately gather it back.
One must make the aware mind focused, continuous, and sustained. When the practice becomes familiar, one can anchor on the dharma-realm even amid activity. The Mañjuśrī Prajñā Sūtra says:

“The dharma-realm is one characteristic; to anchor the mind on the dharma-realm is called one-practice samādhi. … One who enters one-practice samādhi knows all Buddhas and the dharma-realm, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to be without distinction.”

Question: Concretely, how should one observe and illumine so as to accomplish “within, not turning with thoughts; without, not pulled by circumstances; not grasping at characteristics, and unmoved in suchness”?
Answer: All the many methods described above can accomplish it. Try them more, and choose the one most effective for you. In addition, you may also investigate a huatou:
What is the present thought?

In this way you will for longer and longer periods abide in a state that is thought-free yet aware. If deluded thoughts arise, you will see them at once. If a deluded thought arises, look: does it contain greed, anger, or delusion? Does it turn with the thought (producing thought upon thought)? Is it pulled by circumstances? Does it cling to characteristics and become moved by them? When a deluded thought arises, this is karma binding the mind; to dissolve it is the mind turning karma.
Accomplish “not letting a single thought slip past, penetrating every thought.”

By constantly breaking up and dissolving the invasions of deluded thoughts, the power to subdue afflictions grows ever greater and karmic hindrances grow ever thinner. When the work is deep, karma dissolves and wisdom shines; hindrances end and blessings mount—a joy beyond words.

Therefore, in practice one should take awakening as the foundation, remain alert in every thought, contemplate the five desires and six objects as dream, illusion, and empty flower, and see greed, anger, delusion, and all the various ordinary mind-states with perfect clarity, so as to not turn with thoughts and not be pulled by circumstances
, not grasp at characteristics, and remain unmoved in suchness
The Mahāvairocana Sūtra says:
“What is bodhi? It is knowing one’s own mind as it truly is.”

Its commentary says: “‘Knowing one’s own mind as it truly is’ is precisely the opening up and revealing of the treasury of the Tathāgata’s merits. It is like a person who, though he has heard of a treasure, sets his mind to seeking it diligently—if he does not know where it is, he has no way to proceed. … Where is this Dharma to be obtained? It is the practitioner’s own mind. If one can observe it as it truly is and clearly realize and know it, this is called attaining bodhi. In truth it is not awakened by another, not obtained from another. Question: If the mind itself is the Way, why do sentient beings revolve in birth and death and fail to become Buddhas? Answer: Because they do not know it as it truly is.’ The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“Sitting in stillness in mountain forests, cultivating the lower, middle, and higher, one can see the flow of one’s own mind’s deluded projections.”
Master Hanshan said: “This is truly the World-Honored One’s direct instruction on the key method of doing the work.” (Mengyou Ji, “Informal Talk at Jingshan Chan Hall”)
[Yan zuo: to sit silently in stillness.]

blocks.text: 3. Breaking Through the Final Pass (Cutting Off Afflictions)

inline.s: The core of breaking through the final pass is to accomplish: effortless freedom, giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing (the thoughts that arise are free of greed, anger, and delusion).
At this stage one must
do the work of “the mind not forcing names,” in order to attain
freedom from discriminating views
. The Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, says:
“Circumstances and conditions have no beauty or ugliness
(circumstances and conditions are neither good nor bad)
; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not force names
(if the mind does not insistently discriminate good from bad)
, whence would deluded feelings arise? Since deluded feelings do not arise, the true mind knows all freely.”

[Circumstances and conditions have no beauty or ugliness: circumstances and conditions are all illusions—how could an illusion be called good or bad, beautiful or ugly? The “ugliness” here means “bad.” The Heart Sūtra says: “All dharmas are marked with emptiness: they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.”] [Beauty and ugliness arise from the mind: good or bad—both come about because the mind takes circumstances and conditions as real and so makes this discrimination.] [If the mind does not force names, whence would deluded feelings arise: if the mind does not impose good or bad upon the various circumstances and conditions that are inherently without discrimination, whence would the deluded feelings of liking, disliking, taking, and rejecting arise?]

The deluded feelings of love and hate, taking and rejecting, are the root of birth-and-death and saṃsāra; and these deluded feelings arise from taking the illusion of circumstances and conditions as real and discriminating it as good or bad. Therefore the key to ending birth and death and escaping saṃsāra is that the mind not force names and be without discrimination. One must penetrate and see that all dharmas are illusion, nonexistent, unobtainable. “Because nothing is obtained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñāpāramitā, has no hindrance in the mind. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; far removed from inverted dreams, he reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.” (The Heart Sūtra) Therefore the practice at this stage is to
be free from discriminating views

with all one’s effort. “Knowing illusion, one is immediately free, without resorting to means; being free of illusion, one is immediately awake, with no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who practice thus will forever be free of all illusions.” (The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment)
Question: Why should
the mind not discriminate good and ugly

Answer: The very instant when faculty and object meet is the primordial state—no intention, no discrimination. If one discriminates beauty and ugliness, one begins to spin deluded thoughts; what follows is affliction, then karma-making, and so there is birth-and-death and saṃsāra.
Question: Why is that?
Answer:

This is because as soon as one discriminates beauty and ugliness (good or bad), there is love and hate; where there is love and hate, there is taking and rejecting; where there is taking and rejecting (in thought and in action), karma is made—this is the root of birth and death. Therefore one should “in seeing, just seeing; in hearing, just hearing; in knowing, just knowing; in being aware, just being aware,” and not give rise to thoughts of love and hate, taking and rejecting.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“Bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas, relying on the noble teachings, are without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet seclusion, they observe self-awakening, not awakened by another,
free from discriminating views
, and step by step advance upward, entering the Tathāgata’s ground. Such practice is called the aspect of practicing the self-realized noble wisdom.”

[Noble wisdom: the wisdom that, like principle, correctly illumines the ultimate truth and is free of false discrimination, is called noble wisdom. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra’s preface by Sengzhao says: “Noble wisdom is without knowing, yet illumines all things; the dharmakāya is without form, yet responds to every shape.”] [Ultimate truth: also called the supreme-meaning truth or the truth of the highest meaning—the true principle known and seen by noble wisdom, that is, the inwardly realized dharma-nature beyond words. The true principle known and seen by noble wisdom is free of all falseness, hence it is called “true”; its principle is eternal and unchanging, hence it is called “truth.”] [Aspect of practice: the manner in which practice is carried out.]
It also says:
“What is called the aspect of the One Vehicle practice? It means realizing and knowing the One Vehicle path. What is called knowing the One Vehicle path? It is
free from the discrimination of the grasping subject and the grasped object
, dwelling as it truly is.”

[One Vehicle: the only teaching that can bring people to Buddhahood. “Vehicle” means a carriage; it is used to liken the Buddha’s teaching, which can carry people to the far shore of nirvāṇa—hence it is called a “vehicle.”]
The Wudeng Huiyuan records: the Chan
Fourth Patriarch Daoxin instructed Farong, saying:
“The hundred thousand Dharma gates all return to the square inch
(the mind)

; the wondrous virtues, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all in the mind-source. All gates of precepts, of samādhi, of wisdom, and all spiritual transformations are complete in themselves, not apart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic hindrances are originally empty and still; all causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no threefold world to escape, no bodhi to seek. Humans and non-humans are equal in nature and characteristics. The great Way is vast
(empty)
and boundless, beyond thought and beyond deliberation. Such a Dharma you have now obtained, lacking
(missing)

nothing—how are you different from a Buddha? There is no other Dharma. Simply let the mind be free; do not practice contemplation, do not still the mind, do not give rise to greed or anger, do not harbor sorrow or worry. Vast and unobstructed, let yourself roam at will. Do not do good deeds, do not do evil deeds. Walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever your eyes meet and whatever conditions you encounter are all the Buddha’s wondrous function. Happy and without care—this is what is called Buddha.”

[Farong (594–657): founder of the Oxhead school.] [Mind-source: the mind is the source of all dharmas, hence “mind-source.” The Bodhicitta Śāstra says: “If deluded thoughts arise, know them and do not follow. When delusions cease, the mind-source is empty and still. Ten thousand virtues are complete, and its wondrous function is inexhaustible.” The Mohe Zhiguan says: “Cross-legged with hands folded, lips sealed and tongue still, contemplate the true reality; the mind-source is at one and still, and the dharma-realm is equally still.” It also says: “If one wishes to illumine and know, one must know the mind-source. If the mind-source is non-dual, then all dharmas are alike as empty space.”] [Non-human: refers to the eight classes of heavenly dragons and others who are not human, as well as yakṣas, evil ghosts, asuras, hell-beings, and so on. It is also generally used as a general term for ghosts and spirits.] [Freedom: the mind is free from the bonds of affliction and penetrates everywhere without obstruction—this is called freedom. The Lotus Sūtra, “Introductory Chapter,” says: “All bonds of existence exhausted, the mind attains freedom.”] [Bonds of existence: “existence” means the karmic retribution of birth and death; “bonds” means the afflictions that can bring about that retribution. Greed, anger, delusion, and the other afflictions can bind a person and keep him within the realm of birth and death, unable to escape; hence they are called bonds of existence.]
The Master
(Farong)
said: ‘Since the mind is complete in itself, what is the Buddha? What is the mind?’ The patriarch said: ‘It is not that the mind cannot ask about the Buddha
(it is not that the mind is unable to ask what the Buddha is)
; to ask about the Buddha is not other than mind
(the very asking what the Buddha is—that is mind)
.’ The Master said: ‘Since contemplation is not permitted, when circumstances arise
(when deluded feelings arise amid circumstances and conditions)
, how should the mind counter them?’ The patriarch said: ‘Circumstances and conditions have no beauty or ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not force names
(if the mind does not insistently name beauty and ugliness)
, whence would deluded feelings arise? Since deluded feelings do not arise, the true mind knows all freely. Simply let yourself be free with the mind
(not forcing names of beauty and ugliness)
, and there is no more countering
(no need to counter deluded feelings anymore)
; this is called the eternally abiding dharmakāya, without change or alteration. I received from Great Master Can
(Sengcan, the Third Patriarch of Chan)
the sudden-teaching Dharma gate, and now I transmit it to you.’

[Simply let yourself be free with the mind, and there is no more countering: you simply let yourself be free with the mind, abiding in a state of awareness without thought and without deliberation, not forcing names of beauty or ugliness upon circumstances and conditions, and then there is no need to counter deluded feelings anymore. Note: to counter deluded feelings is to prune branches and pluck leaves; but for the mind not to force names of beauty or ugliness upon circumstances and conditions is to cut deluded feelings at the root. Since at this stage one has already attained the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one, and is further cultivating the return of the one to nothing, one has the capacity to accomplish “the mind not forcing names”—one need only temper and elevate it amid circumstances and conditions, until it becomes effortless and non-doing.]

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, according to conformity with the awakened nature, divides the differences in what is realized into four levels: 1. the ordinary person’s conformity with the awakened nature; 2. the conformity of bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the grounds; 3. the conformity of bodhisattvas who have entered the grounds; 4. the Tathāgata’s conformity with the awakened nature. The sutra says:

Good sons! All sentient beings, from beginningless time, because of the deluded thought of a self and of one who loves that self, have never themselves known the arising and ceasing of thought after thought, and so give rise to hate and love and become attached to the five desires. If they meet a good friend who teaches them to awaken to the pure and perfect enlightened nature, and they understand arising and ceasing, they then know that this life is by nature wearisome toil. If there are those in whom wearisome toil is forever ended and who attain the purity of the dharma-realm, then that very understanding of purity becomes an obstruction to themselves, and so they are not at ease in perfect enlightenment. This is called the ordinary person’s conformity with the awakened nature.

[Wearisome toil forever ended, attaining the purity of the dharma-realm, and that very understanding of purity becoming an obstruction to oneself, and so not being at ease in perfect enlightenment: Master Hanshan’s Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “When a person has completely subdued the five abidings and first cut off the delusions of views and thoughts, this is what is meant by ‘wearisome toil forever ended.’ The three poisons no longer function, so it is said ‘he attains the purity of the dharma-realm.’ He is attached to the pure state, so it is said ‘the understanding of purity is an obstruction.’ Ignorance (fundamental ignorance) remains entirely, ‘and so he is not at ease in perfect enlightenment.’”] [Five abidings: an abbreviation of the five abiding-place delusions.] [The five abiding-place delusions: the five abidings are: the delusion of views in the three realms as one abiding; the delusion of thought in the three realms divided into three abidings; fundamental ignorance as one abiding—together making five abidings. Because these five delusions cause sentient beings to abide in and cling to birth and death, they are called abiding places. (The three realms are the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.)]

Good sons! All bodhisattvas see understanding as an obstruction; though they cut off the obstruction of understanding, they still abide in the awareness of seeing, and the obstruction of that awareness is an obstruction, so they are not at ease. This is called the conformity with the awakened nature of bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the grounds.

[Not yet entered the grounds: not yet entered the ten grounds.] [Ten grounds: among the fifty-two stages of bodhisattva practice, the fifth set of ten is called the ten grounds. In these ten grounds one gradually opens the Buddha realm and accomplishes all-aspect wisdom; this already belongs to the noble stages, hence it is also called the “ten nobles.”] [All-aspect wisdom: the wisdom that penetrates both the general and the particular characteristics of all dharmas, and that transforms beings and cuts off delusion.]

Good sons! To have illumination and awareness is in every case called an obstruction. Therefore the bodhisattva, constantly aware yet not abiding, sees both the illumination and the one who illumines simultaneously become still and extinct. It is like a person who cuts off his own head: once the head is cut off, there is no one who can cut. Then, with the obstruction-creating mind, one extinguishes all obstructions; once the obstructions are cut off and extinguished, there is no one who extinguishes obstructions. The sutra teachings are like a finger pointing at the moon: if one then sees the moon, one understands that what is pointed at is after all not the moon. The various words and instructions by which all Tathāgatas reveal to bodhisattvas are likewise so. This is called the conformity with the awakened nature of bodhisattvas who have entered the grounds.

[Xiuduo luo (sūtra): translated into Chinese as “conforming scripture.” “Conforming” means that above it conforms to the wondrous principle of all Buddhas, and below it conforms to the capacities of sentient beings; “scripture” means a thread, threading together the meanings of the Dharma so they are not scattered and lost.]

Good sons! All obstructions are ultimate enlightenment; gaining a thought or losing a thought is in every case liberation; making dharmas or breaking dharmas are both called nirvāṇa; wisdom and folly are equally prajñā; the dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and by non-Buddhists are alike bodhi; ignorance and true suchness are not different states; the precepts, concentration, and wisdom and also lust, anger, and delusion are all pure conduct. Sentient beings and lands are one dharma-nature; hells and heavenly palaces are both Pure Lands; those with nature and those without alike accomplish the Buddha Way; all afflictions are ultimately liberation. The ocean-like wisdom of the dharma-realm illumines all characteristics as like empty space. This is called the Tathāgata’s conformity with the awakened nature.
[Ocean-like wisdom of the dharma-realm: the great wisdom that contemplates the equality of the dharma-realm, deep and wide as the sea—hence the name.]

Good sons! All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; toward all deluded minds they also do not extinguish them; dwelling in the realm of deluded thought, they do not add knowing; in the absence of knowing, they do not dispute what is real. Those sentient beings who hear this Dharma gate, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, and do not give rise to alarm or fear—this is called conformity with the awakened nature.”

[At all times not giving rise to deluded thoughts: “They should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects.”] [Toward all deluded minds also not extinguishing them: “They should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all (that is, they should give rise to a mind free of any dwelling or attachment).”]
Cultivate the root with heart sincere and will upright;
When thoughts arise, follow them not—make this your guiding light.
Take your own nature as the essence; the form-body is not you;
Take spiritual knowing as the mind; deluded thoughts are not true.
When deluded thoughts arise, let none of them be followed;
At death’s hour karma cannot bind you; wherever you wish, you go.
Master Guifeng says:
“There is no sentient being who does not possess the awakened nature, spiritually bright, empty, and still, no different from a Buddha. But because
(owing to the fact that)

since beginningless kalpas they have never understood or awakened, they deludedly cling to the body as the mark of a self, and so give rise to feelings of love and hate. Following feeling they create karma; following karma they receive retribution—birth, old age, sickness, and death, revolving for long kalpas. Yet the awakened nature within the body has never been born or died; it is like being driven about in a dream while the body itself remains at ease, or like water becoming ice while its wet nature does not change. If one can awaken to this nature
(the awakened nature)

as being the dharmakāya, originally unborn, what support could it need? Spiritually bright and undimmed, clearly and constantly knowing, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Yet through many lives of deluded clinging, habit has become nature; joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure flow on in subtle streams. Though the truth may be suddenly penetrated, these feelings are hard to cast off at once; one must constantly be aware and watch, reducing and reducing again. It is like the wind suddenly stopping while the waves gradually subside—how could the practice of one lifetime equal the power and function of all Buddhas? One need only take empty stillness as one’s own substance and not mistake the form-body for oneself; take spiritual knowing as one’s own mind and not mistake deluded thoughts for it.
When deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them
(do not follow any of them)
; then at the time of death, karma will naturally be unable to bind you.

Though there is an intermediate existence, you go wherever you wish—in heaven or among humans, taking birth as you please. If thoughts of love and hate are already extinguished, then one no longer receives a body subject to fragmentary birth and death
(no longer subject to fragmentary birth and death)

, and can naturally change the short for the long, the coarse for the subtle. If the subtle streams are all stilled and extinguished, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone in clarity, then one responds to capacities and manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies to save sentient beings with the karmic connection—this is called a Buddha.”
(Jingde Chuandeng Lu)

[Taking empty stillness as one’s own substance: this is spoken from the ultimate point of view. Since awareness Chan is concerned with ending fragmentary birth and death, it takes self-nature as the substance, which makes it easier to understand and grasp.] [Spiritual knowing: that is, the knowing of empty stillness.] [Intermediate existence: the intermediate-existence body, also called the “in-between,” is a transformation body formed of subtle matter that sustains life after a person dies but before taking rebirth; this transformation body is the intermediate-existence body. During the first forty-nine days, this intermediate-existence body undergoes one birth and death every seven days, passing through seven such births and deaths, waiting for the arrangement of karmic conditions before going to take rebirth.]
Here three levels of practice are described:

1. Subduing afflictions. Its requirement is: when deluded thoughts arise, do not follow any of them. (Please pay special attention to the word “any.”) Its effect is: at the time of death, karma cannot bind you; though there is an intermediate existence, you go wherever you wish—in heaven or among humans, taking birth as you please.

2. Cutting off afflictions. Its requirement is: thoughts of love and hate are already extinguished. Its effect is: ending birth and death (no longer subject to fragmentary birth and death), and escaping the three realms.

3. Realizing the Buddha fruit. Its requirement is: the subtle streams are all stilled and extinguished, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone in clarity. Its effect is: no longer subject to transformational birth and death, responding to capacities and manifesting hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies to save sentient beings with the karmic connection—this is called a Buddha.
Master Guifeng also says:

All dharmas are like dreams—all sages say the same. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and the objects of the senses are originally empty. The mind of empty stillness is spiritually knowing and undimmed.
This very knowing of empty stillness is your true nature.

Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor does it come into being because of objects. The single word “knowing” is the gate of all wonders. Because of beginningless delusion, one deludedly clings to body and mind as “I” and gives rise to thoughts of greed and anger. If one meets a good friend who reveals it, one suddenly awakens to the knowing of empty stillness. Knowing is without thought and without form—who then is the mark of a self, the mark of a person?
Awakening to the emptiness of all characteristics, the mind is naturally without thought
As soon as a thought arises, be aware; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.

Therefore, though one cultivates all myriad practices, one takes no-thought as the essence. Once one has the knowledge and vision of no-thought, love and hate naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase and brighten, karmic offenses naturally are cut off, and one’s practice naturally advances. Having understood that all characteristics are not characteristics, one naturally practices without practicing. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are ended. When arising and ceasing have ceased, stillness and illumination appear before one, functioning inexhaustibly—this is called a Buddha.
Preface to the Collected Writings on the Source of Chan
As to whether one can be master of oneself at the time of death, Master Guifeng’s verse says
(see the Jingde Chuandeng Lu)
To do deeds of meaning
this is the awakened mind
To do deeds without meaning
this is the crazed and disordered mind
It also says:
Crazed and disordered, following feeling and thought, at death one is dragged by karma;
The awakened do not follow feeling; at death they can turn karma.
Now the two verses are annotated as follows:

The first verse sets forth the causes of karma that are created. At the moment when the mind stirs and a thought arises, whether one follows feeling or relies on wisdom (the wisdom that awakens to principle)—this is the watershed between delusion and awakening.
To do deeds of meaning
this is the awakened mind
To do deeds of meaning—this is the awakened mind.
“Meaning”
means
the principle of what is right
Whatever
one
undertakes
one should
first
carefully
weigh right and wrong,
benefit and harm
. One
must
conform to
that principle
and only then act—this is the awakened mind,
not
the
same as
the drunken and crazed
In terms of the Buddhadharma
there are three kinds of meaningful deeds that may be done
. Those that
benefit
the health of
the physical body,
such as
clothing and food
medicine
and shelter—worldly meaningful
deeds;
. Those that
benefit
the realization of
the dharmakāya
—deeds
such as
precepts, concentration, and wisdom
and the six pāramitās—supreme-meaning
deeds;
Upholding
and spreading
the true Dharma
benefiting and saving living beings
. That is, the three tasks of sustaining life, practicing, and spreading the Dharma.
[Xingwu: awakening.]
To do deeds without meaning
this is the crazed and disordered mind
To do deeds without meaning—this is the crazed and disordered mind.
Whatever
one
does
if it is not connected with
the above
three kinds of meaningful deeds, it is called a deed without meaning
. This is to waste energy and time for nothing, and even to create evil karma. Such
a crazed and disordered person
is then
like the drunkards and madmen of the world, who go anywhere without choosing a place, do anything without weighing right and wrong
choose neither meaning nor benefit, and merely give free rein to feeling and deluded calculation
doing whatever they please—
this is
the crazed
and disordered mind.
The second
verse
sets forth
the
retribution received
. Those who act following feeling are bound by karma at death and receive birth according to karma; those who act relying on wisdom are free at death and not bound by karma.
